item.title: Musk chose to restrict Ukraine's access to SpaceX network, sources say
item.description:
A decision by Elon Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, people familiar with the matter told CBS News.
The satellite service, which is used for drone operations, hitting certain targets and protecting sites in Ukraine, was slowed significantly last week.
Musk held multiple conversations with administration officials leading up to the order, the sources said. He wanted clarity on the president's thinking on the matter. Musk has expressed distaste with his company being seen as profiting from the continued war between Russia and Ukraine.
It's not clear how Musk's order to curtail service was executed.
Musk licenses SpaceX's Starshield technology to the U.S. government. He said last week the U.S. controls who can access the technology and what level of service those users receive.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk, the world's richest person, wrote on X.
Musk did not reply to a request for comment. CBS News has reached out to the White House and the Pentagon for comment.
The Wall Street Journal was first to report on Musk's order.
The temporary restrictions came as a surprise to some officials inside the administration, who said neither Mr. Trump nor the Pentagon specifically ordered any limits meant to deliberately disrupt drone operations and battlefield communications.
Mr. Trump said Monday he was seeking details on who ordered the slowdown.
"I don't know who it was, but I'd like to find out," he said.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Tuesday the Pentagon has not manipulated the service.
"We haven't pulled anything back. There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to. And that's where Starlink has the option to make those decisions, but nothing's changed from our view. We haven't made any directives or anything like that," Hegseth told reporters, adding that "we wish the Ukrainians, obviou...

item.title: Iran touts closest ever ties with Russia, contradicting Trump
item.description:
What to know about the Iran war today: Iran's foreign minister said Tuesday that Tehran's ties with Russia had never been so close, after President Trump said Moscow was "doing very little, if anything, to help" Iran amid the war in the Middle East. Russia's foreign minister, on his first visit to Tehran this week since the outbreak of the war, called U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran illegal.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu shared a video Monday on social media of a phone call with Mr. Trump during which he suggests possible new joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran, telling the American leader they have "a job to finish." U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth met with Netanyahu on Monday during an unannounced visit to Israel, according to two sources familiar with the matter.

item.title: French government extends curfews after riots sweep across the country
item.description:
French authorities are extending curfews and increasing the police presence in public spaces as President Emmanuel Macron's government tries to regain control after rioters torched buildings and looted thousands of businesses this weekend.
But addressing the problems that have brought students and workers to the streets for the last five weeks will be a tougher proposition.
Protesters are demanding better schools and relief from rising living costs, while the government faces mounting debt and a fractured parliament that makes even passing a budget difficult.
RATP transport security officers and RATP staff stand inside the closed off Republique Metro station during a partial curfew for parts of Paris on Oct. 20, 2026, after weekend demonstrations over soaring prices degenerated into some of the worst street violence in recent years.
SIMON WOHLFAHRT /AFP via Getty Images
More police and curfews
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu promised a "massive" police deployment Tuesday ahead of the next demonstrations scheduled for Oct. 24. The announcement followed Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez's acknowledgment that authorities had underestimated the unrest and lost control in some cities during Saturday's protests.
More than 2,500 people had been taken into police custody by Monday evening, Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said, after violence that included the burning of a historic town hall in Limoges, a city in central France.
Overnight curfews have been imposed around Paris' Place de la République and Les Halles shopping district, with restrictions also introduced in Lyon and other cities. Paris and Lyon reported no major incidents Monday night, and authorities are extending the measures.

item.title: Hegseth meets Netanyahu ahead of elections, possible Iran war restart
item.description:
Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth quietly visited Israel on Monday and met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, according to a senior U.S. military official who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
A second source involved in the matter in Israel confirmed Tuesday morning that Netanyahu met Hegseth.
The unannounced visit came just over a week before Netanyahu's party faces elections. It also comes after President Trump floated resuming military operations against Iran following next month's U.S. midterm elections.
Hegseth confirmed the visit in comments to reporters Tuesday, saying he "was there visiting our troops" and "had a chance to talk to the prime minister."
"Of course, the nature of our conversations is not something I would talk about but they've been good partners and I appreciate that," Hegseth said.
The Pentagon declined to comment on the visit. CBS News has reached out to the Israeli government for comment.
Axios was first to report Hegseth's visit.
Israeli and U.S. forces jointly launched strikes against Iran in late February, and the two allies worked closely with each other early in the war. The U.S. also struck three Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025 during a broader conflict between Israel and Iran.
Iran and the U.S. have largely refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, but Mr. Trump has said openly that he is still weighing whether to cut a deal with Iran's leadership or "annihilate" the country — a decision he says could come after the November midterm elections.
Netanyahu, the longest-serving prime minister in Israeli history, faces his own political uncertainty a week from Tuesday. The coalition led by his right-wing Likud party is seeking to remain in power, but it faces several more centrist challengers, including one party run by former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot.

item.title: U.S. ramps up warnings to Americans in Middle East after Houthi strikes
item.description:
U.S. diplomatic missions across the Middle East have issued a new round of security warnings to Americans amid escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants against Saudi Arabia, including an Oct. 10 strike on Riyadh's international airport that killed an American citizen.
The alerts, issued Sunday by U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and several other countries, warned that hostilities could rapidly and without warning spread beyond areas already affected by the fighting. The advisories urged Americans to exercise vigilance and prepare for possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions.
"We are actively warning U.S. citizens about the very real threat the Houthis pose and urging them to heed official guidance," Edgar Vasquez, the State Department's deputy assistant secretary for press, told CBS News.
"These alerts are part of a proactive effort by the Trump administration to ensure Americans are aware of potential risks," Vasquez said, adding that the safety and security of American citizens remain the department's "top priority."
The State Department has maintained restrictions on diplomatic operations across parts of the region since the U.S. and Israel went to war with Iran in February. State Department officials have said the restrictions are intended to be temporary and allow embassies to adjust staffing as security conditions evolve.
Under a longstanding "no double standard" policy, embassies are required to share security threat information with private American citizens when the same risks apply to U.S. diplomatic personnel.
The latest alerts follow a surge in Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, including repeated strikes on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and oil facilities belonging to Saudi Aramco. The Oct. 10 airport attack killed at least 13 people and injured more than 300, according to Saudi authorities.

item.title: 2 men rearrested for alleged spying for Iran in U.K. air base incident
item.description:
British police said Tuesday they have rearrested two men on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service over the suspected plot at a U.S.-run air base in England last month.
Counter Terrorism Policing said the men, a 24-year-old British national and a 25-year-old dual U.K.-Iranian national, were arrested under the National Security Act.
The men were earlier arrested but had been bailed pending more investigation.
Police are investigating a suspected terror plot on Sept. 27 against the U.S.-run base at RAF Fairford in western England, which has been used to bomb Iran during this year's war.
Scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the base as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area. Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant - gasoline - in three vans at the site, but no explosives.
British authorities have linked Tehran to the incident, which led the U.S. to pull its bombers from RAF Fairford.
Five other men who were also arrested earlier remain on bail. No one has yet been charged.
Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the U.K., said detectives are looking at "many lines of enquiry involved in this hugely complex investigation."
"This is very much a live investigation, and our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement," he said in a statement.
"Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it," he added.
Iranian officials have said several times since the beginning of the war that any bases used to attack the country would be considered legitimate targets.
